item.title: Behavioural Environmental Economics & Policy (BEEP): trends and reflections
item.content:encoded:
Sanchayan Banerjee, King's College London

Lory Barile, University of Warwick

Behavioural Environmental Economics & Policy (BEEP) addresses how departures from rational choice assumptions affect environmental policy effectiveness. While traditional approaches rely on regulation and price-based instruments, behavioural research reveals that bounded rationality creates failures that can undermine policy outcomes. This special issue consolidates evidence on how behavioural insights improve environmental policy design, delivery, and evaluation.

The issue welcomes theoretical, empirical, and policy-oriented contributions that apply behavioural approaches to environmental challenges including climate change, biodiversity loss, and pollution. Contributors should diagnose how market and behavioural failures interact, and design and test policies combining traditional instruments with behavioural tools such as defaults, framing, and commitment devices.

The collection serves practitioners and researchers by providing evidence-based guidance on implementing behavioural insights in environmental policy, with emphasis on welfare implications, distributional equity, and the effectiveness of green nudges.

Appel publié par Environmental and Resource Economics. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Market failures and behavioural failures in environmental settings
  • Policy design combining prices/standards with behavioural tools
  • Welfare analysis, ethics, and paternalism in environmental policy
  • Empirical identification of behavioural mechanisms
  • Heterogeneity, equity, and distributional consequences
  • Replication, meta-analysis, and open-science practices
  • Choice architecture and environmental outcomes
  • Climate cognition and communication
  • Evaluation and methods

Timeline

item.title: Wildfires in a Changing Climate: Impacts, Adaptation, and Policy
item.content:encoded:
Robert J. R. Elliott, University of Birmingham

Sarah Meier, ETH Zurich

Eric Strobl, University of Bern

Wildfires are increasingly posing systemic economic and ecological risks as fire seasons lengthen and intensity increases. The economic consequences extend beyond direct suppression costs to include supply chain disruptions, reduced labour productivity, impacts on tourism, altered housing markets, and substantial public health burdens from smoke exposure. Current policies are insufficient to address these evolving challenges.

This special issue seeks empirical research that quantifies the economic welfare impacts of wildfires and evaluates the effectiveness of emerging adaptation strategies. The collection welcomes studies using innovative data sources to understand wildfire impacts across diverse regions, particularly those facing emerging risks. Research should span impact assessment and policy evaluation, from labour market effects and insurance mechanisms to ecosystem valuation and monitoring technologies.

Potential topics

  • Labour productivity and sectoral employment shifts
  • Housing markets and migration responses
  • Natural capital and ecosystem service valuation
  • Inequality and distributional impacts
  • Public finance and insurance markets
  • Governance and risk-sharing arrangements
  • Prevention and suppression strategies
  • Smoke exposure and health outcomes

item.title: Market-Based Measures for Port and Shipping Emissions Mitigation
item.content:encoded:
This special issue focuses on market-based measures and economic instruments designed to mitigate emissions from ports and the shipping industry. The collection seeks to advance understanding of how market mechanisms can effectively reduce environmental impacts while maintaining economic competitiveness in the maritime sector.

The issue welcomes contributions exploring various market-based approaches including carbon pricing, emission trading systems, green bonds, subsidies for clean technologies, and other economic instruments. Papers may examine these mechanisms from theoretical, empirical, or policy perspectives, with particular interest in their effectiveness, design, implementation challenges, and real-world outcomes.

Appel publié par Transportation Research Part D Transport and Environment. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Market-based mechanisms for reducing port and shipping emissions
  • Carbon pricing and emission trading systems in maritime transport
  • Economic instruments for incentivizing sustainable shipping practices
  • Port authority policies and market-based approaches
  • Life cycle assessment and environmental impact of shipping
  • Technological innovations and market adoption in emissions reduction
  • Regulatory frameworks and market-based policy integration
  • Case studies of successful market-based emissions mitigation strategies

Timeline

  • August 28, 2026: Manuscript submission deadline
